question1.question: A pull request modifies 14 files across the stock tracking module. Your single-pass review analyzing all files together produces inconsistent results: detailed feedback for some files but superficial comments for others, obvious bugs missed, and contradictory feedback—flagging a pattern as problematic in one file while approving identical code elsewhere in the same PR. How should you restructure the review?
answers: A. Run three independent review passes across all 14 files simultaneously, then consolidate only findings that appear in at least two of the three passes to reduce noise and inconsistency.
B. Switch to a higher-tier model with a 200k-token context window capable of holding all 14 files simultaneously and producing uniform attention across every section of the pull request.
C. Require developers to split large pull requests into batches of 3–4 files each before submitting, so the automated review can analyze each batch thoroughly in a single focused pass.
D. Split into focused passes: analyze each file individually for local issues, then run a separate integration-focused pass examining cross-file data flow.

question1.question: Your review agent processes an entire microservice migration PR—22 files—in one shot. Output quality is inconsistent: some modules receive detailed analysis, others get one-line summaries, and feedback contradicts itself across files. The context window is not exceeded. What is the most likely root cause and fix?
answers: A. The model degrades in quality when given insufficient processing time for multi-file inputs; increasing the pipeline timeout parameter would allow it to complete consistent, thorough reviews.
B. Attention quality degrades when many files share a single context; split into per-file passes plus a separate integration pass.
C. The prompt lacks är output consistency.

question1.question: A team member proposes solving inconsistent multi-file PR reviews by switching to a model with a 200k-token context window, arguing it can hold all files at once and produce uniform analysis. What is the fundamental flaw in this reasoning?
answers: A. The proposal is entirely valid — a 200k-token model holds all files simultaneously and distributes attention equally across every section for uniform, consistent feedback.
B. 200k-token models are prohibitively expensive for high-frequency CI/CD pipelines, and the marginal improvement in review quality cannot justify the increased per-request cost.
C. A larger context window does not fix attention degradation across many files; focused per-file passes are still needed.
D. Larger context windows significantly increase model inference latency, pushing automated review turnaround times beyond acceptable thresholds for blocking pull request workflows.

question1.question: When a Claude-based review system produces inconsistent output quality across a large input divided into many sections, what structural change most reliably improves consistency?
answers: A. Retry each inconsistently reviewed section with a higher temperature setting, using the increased output variance to eventually produce more thorough and complete feedback.
B. Add explicit consistency instructions directing the model to maintain equal analysis depth across every section, and flag any section it cannot review comprehensively.
C. Reduce overall input size by summarizing each section to a fixed token budget before analysis, ensuring no single section dominates the model's attention capacity.
D. Replace the single large prompt with decomposed focused prompts, each covering a specific subset or concern.

question2.question: Your automated reviews identify valid issues but developers report the feedback isn't actionable. Findings say things like 'complex ticket allocation logic' or 'potential null pointer' without specifying what to change. When you add detailed instructions like 'always include specific fix suggestions,' the model still produces inconsistent output—sometimes detailed, sometimes vague. What prompting technique would most reliably produce consistently actionable feedback?
answers: A. Expand the context window to include more of the surrounding codebase so the model has sufficient information to suggest specific fixes.
B. Add 3–4 few-shot examples showing the exact format you want: issue identified, code location, specific fix suggestion.
C. Implement a two-pass approach where one prompt identifies issues and a second prompt generates fixes, allowing specialization.
D. Further refine the instructions with more explicit requirements for each part of the feedback format.

question2.question: A documentation generator produces inconsistently formatted API docs despite a prompt that says 'always include parameters, return type, and example usage.' Some functions get all three; others only get a description. Explicit instructions haven't fixed it. What change would most reliably produce uniform output?
answers: A. Increase the model temperature to produce more varied and complete outputs, relying on higher randomness to surface all required documentation components.
B. Decompose the task into three focused prompts — one each for parameters, return type, and usage examples — allowing each sub-task to generate a single component reliably.
C. Add few-shot examples showing exactly what complete, correctly formatted docs look like for 3–4 functions.
D. Implement an automated output validator that checks for all three required documentation components and triggers automatic retries until a complete response is returned.

question2.question: A developer tries to fix inconsistent review output by writing increasingly detailed instructions: 'always include the exact line number,' 'always suggest the specific fix,' 'never omit the severity rating.' Despite five rounds of instruction refinement, output remains inconsistent. Why isn't this approach working?
answers: A. The model silently discards prompt instructions beyond a certain total character count, so each additional formatting refinement has no measurable effect on its output behavior.
B. The prompt is missing a system-role declaration that activates the model's instruction-following mode; without it, all formatting directives are treated as optional suggestions.
C. The instructions target the wrong layer — they describe the desired format but never demonstrate it through examples.
D. Instruction-based format enforcement only works reliably with models specifically fine-tuned for structured output; general-purpose models require in-prompt demonstrations instead.

question2.question: What is the most reliable way to get a language model to produce output in a specific, consistent format when explicit instructions alone have failed to produce consistency?
answers: A. Constrain the output using a JSON schema or regex validation and retry on failure.
B. Provide demonstrations of the desired format through few-shot examples embedded within the prompt.
C. Simplify format requirements incrementally, removing optional fields until the model reliably produces minimal structure before adding complexity back.
D. Increase the length and specificity of formatting instructions, adding explicit rules for each required field and concrete examples of malformed output to avoid.

question3.question: Your automated code review system shows inconsistent severity ratings—similar issues like null pointer risks receive 'critical' severity in some PRs but only 'medium' in others. Developer trust is declining because teams can't predict which findings require immediate attention. What's the most effective way to improve severity consistency?
answers: A. Add a CLAUDE.md file that lists issue types and their default severities, instructing Claude to reference this mapping when assigning ratings.
B. Modify the prompt to ask Claude to rate severity relative to other issues in the same PR, so the most severe issue is always marked critical.
C. Request that Claude include its reasoning for each severity assignment, then use that reasoning to manually calibrate and adjust ratings during review.
D. Include explicit severity criteria in your prompt with concrete code examples for each severity level.

question3.question: A Claude-based bug classifier labels identical exception patterns as 'high priority' in one service and 'low priority' in another. The prompt says 'rate priority based on potential user impact' but gives no further guidance. What change would most improve rating consistency?
answers: A. Add a hardcoded rule requiring all unhandled exceptions to be marked as high priority, using exception type as a reliable proxy for potential user impact.
B. Instruct the model to compare findings across all services before assigning priority, using relative severity ranking as the calibration mechanism.
C. Implement a post-processing normalization step that redistributes priority labels to match a fixed target ratio, overriding the model's contextual judgment.
D. Define each priority level with concrete examples of code patterns that qualify for that level.

question3.question: A team tries to fix inconsistent severity ratings by asking Claude to always 'justify its severity choice' in the output. After a week, severity inconsistency persists even though justifications are now included. Why did this approach fail?
answers: A. Requiring justification documents the existing inconsistent reasoning rather than anchoring ratings to defined criteria.
B. Justifications increase output length, which degrades model performance on classification tasks.
C. Claude cannot justify severity because it has no access to historical bug impact data.
D. The approach would have worked if the team had combined it with a stricter system prompt.

question3.question: What is the most effective way to reduce variance in a language model's categorical classifications (e.g., severity, priority, confidence) when the model produces inconsistent labels for similar inputs?
answers: A. Average results across multiple runs and use the most common classification.
B. Add a calibration prompt that runs before each request to prime the model's rating scale.
C. Define clear classification boundaries with representative examples of inputs at each level, embedded directly in the prompt.
D. Reduce the number of classification levels to binary (high/low) to simplify the decision.

question4.question: Your CI/CD system performs three types of Claude-powered analysis: (1) quick style checks on each PR that block merging until complete, (2) comprehensive security audits of the entire codebase run weekly, and (3) test case generation triggered nightly for recently-modified modules. The Message Batches API offers 50% cost savings but can take up to 24 hours to process. Which combination correctly matches each task to its API approach?
answers: A. Use synchronous calls for all three tasks for consistent response times, and rely on prompt caching to reduce costs across all workloads.
B. Use synchronous calls for PR style checks and nightly test generation; use Message Batches API only for weekly security audits.
C. Use synchronous calls for PR style checks; use the Message Batches API for weekly security audits and nightly test generation.
D. Use the Message Batches API for all three tasks to maximize the 50% cost savings, and configure the pipeline to poll for batch completion.

question4.question: An engineering platform runs four automated Claude jobs: (A) a linter that blocks CI from proceeding, (B) a monthly cost-attribution report emailed to stakeholders, (C) nightly changelogs generated from merged PRs, (D) on-demand code explanations developers request while coding. The Batch API costs 50% less but returns results asynchronously over hours. Which jobs are the best candidates for batch processing?
answers: A. A and D only — developer-facing tasks need fast responses.
B. B and C only.
C. All four jobs — cost savings apply equally.
D. None — the latency trade-off is unacceptable for automated CI.

question4.question: A team switches all their Claude-powered CI tasks to the Message Batches API to capture the 50% cost savings. Within a day, developers complain that PRs are stuck open for hours waiting for automated feedback. What mistake did the team make?
answers: A. They failed to configure polling correctly, so the pipeline never received batch completion signals.
B. They should have used streaming instead of batch to get faster responses.
C. The Batch API is not supported in CI/CD environments without a separate integration layer.
D. They applied batch processing to latency-sensitive blocking tasks that require real-time responses.

question4.question: When choosing between synchronous and batch API calls for an LLM-powered automation, what is the primary deciding factor?
answers: A. The size of the input — larger inputs should always use batch processing.
B. The frequency of the task — tasks running more than once per day should be synchronous.
C. Whether the result is needed in real time to unblock a downstream process.
D. The model version — newer models support batch; older models require synchronous calls.

question5.question: The code review component works iteratively: Claude analyzes a changed file, then may request related files (imports, base classes, tests) via tool calling to understand context before providing final feedback. Your application defines a tool that lets Claude request file contents; Claude invokes this tool, receives results, and continues its analysis. You're evaluating batch processing to reduce API costs. What is the primary technical constraint when considering batch processing for this workflow?
answers: A. The asynchronous model prevents executing tools mid-request and returning results for Claude to continue analysis.
B. Batch processing lacks request correlation identifiers for matching outputs to input requests.
C. The batch API doesn't support tool definitions in request parameters.
D. Batch processing latency of up to 24 hours is too slow for pull request feedback, though the workflow could otherwise function.

question5.question: An agent that summarizes support tickets first calls a tool to fetch ticket history, incorporates those results, then produces a summary. A developer proposes migrating this agent to batch processing. What technical limitation must they account for?
answers: A. Batch processing limits requests to 1,000 inputs per batch, which may be insufficient.
B. Batch requests lock the conversation state at submission time and cannot incorporate mid-session history from prior turns, preventing multi-turn agents from being processed.
C. The agent's mid-request tool call requires a synchronous response loop that batch processing cannot support.
D. Batch outputs arrive in random order, making it impossible to match summaries to original tickets.

question5.question: A developer argues: 'We can use the Batch API for our tool-calling agent—we'll just include all potentially needed files in the initial request so it never needs to call tools mid-flight.' What is the main problem with this approach?
answers: A. There is no problem with this approach — preloading all relevant files is a valid, efficient workaround that eliminates the need for dynamic tool calls entirely.
B. The Batch API enforces a strict maximum input size per request, making it technically infeasible to include multiple complete source files in a single batch submission.
C. The Batch API explicitly prohibits multi-file inputs by design and accepts only single-file document requests, returning an error on any multi-file payload.
D. Preloading all possible files adds irrelevant context and noise, and you cannot know in advance exactly which files will be needed.

question5.question: Which type of LLM workflow is fundamentally incompatible with asynchronous batch processing?
answers: A. Workflows that generate long-form text output requiring more than 30 seconds to complete.
B. Workflows that run overnight when no developer is present to monitor them.
C. Workflows that process inputs larger than 10,000 tokens per request.
D. Workflows where the model must receive external data mid-execution to continue its reasoning.

question6.question: Your automated review analyzes comments and docstrings. The current prompt instructs Claude to 'check that comments are accurate and up-to-date.' Findings frequently flag acceptable patterns (TODO markers, straightforward descriptions) while missing comments that describe behavior the code no longer implements. What change addresses the root cause of this inconsistent analysis?
answers: A. Filter out TODO, FIXME, and descriptive comment patterns before analysis to reduce noise.
B. Specify explicit criteria: flag comments only when their claimed behavior contradicts actual code behavior.
C. Include git blame data so Claude can identify comments that predate recent code modifications.
D. Add few-shot examples of misleading comments to help the model recognize similar patterns in the codebase.

question6.question: A documentation linter prompt says 'ensure all API docs are complete.' It raises warnings on endpoints that have minimal but accurate docs, while missing endpoints whose docs describe a deprecated request format. What change targets the root cause?
answers: A. Add a minimum word count threshold as the completeness definition, flagging any documentation entry that falls below the required length.
B. Include few-shot examples of fully complete API documentation to help the model recognize and replicate the expected structure and detail level.
C. Include the git history of each doc file so the model can detect stale content.
D. Redefine the check: flag documentation only where the described API contract differs from the actual implementation.

question6.question: To reduce noise in comment analysis, a team adds a pre-filter that strips all TODO and FIXME comments before sending code to Claude. After the change, false positives drop but real issues (code behavior differing from comment description) are still missed. What does this reveal about the original problem?
answers: A. The filter was too aggressive and should be narrowed to only remove FIXME-prefixed comments while preserving TODO markers.
B. The pre-filter approach was fundamentally correct; the remaining misses indicate the model itself requires fine-tuning on this comment type.
C. The filter removed context that Claude relied on to evaluate comment accuracy, creating a performance regression in the behavioral contradiction analysis.
D. The root problem was never the comment types flagged but the absence of a behavioral-contradiction criterion.

question6.question: A quality check prompt produces high false positive rates because its criteria ('is this complete?', 'is this up-to-date?') are vague. What is the most effective type of prompt change to improve precision?
answers: A. Replace vague criteria with operationally precise conditions: 'flag only when X contradicts Y.'
B. Ask the model to rate confidence in each finding and filter out low-confidence results.
C. Add more examples to the prompt to help the model calibrate its judgment.
D. Split the check into multiple smaller prompts to reduce ambiguity per prompt.

question7.question: After an initial automated review generates 12 findings, a developer pushes new commits to address the issues. When the review runs again, it produces 8 findings—but developers report that 5 duplicate earlier comments on code that was already fixed in the new commits. What's the most effective way to eliminate this redundant feedback while maintaining thorough analysis?
answers: A. Run reviews only on initial PR creation and final pre-merge state, skipping intermediate commits.
B. Include prior review findings in context, instructing Claude to only report new or still-unaddressed issues.
C. Restrict the review scope to only files modified in the most recent push, excluding files from earlier commits.
D. Add a post-processing filter that removes findings matching previous file paths and issue descriptions before posting comments.

question7.question: A security scan runs on every CI push. After a developer fixes 3 of 5 flagged vulnerabilities and pushes again, the scan re-flags all 5—including the 2 that were already remediated. The scan prompt has no awareness of prior runs. What is the most direct fix?
answers: A. Limit re-scans to only the newly modified diff lines in the latest push, excluding any file lines that were present in the previous scan.
B. Require developers to manually mark each issue as resolved in the issue tracker before the next automated security scan is triggered.
C. Include the previous scan's findings in the prompt and instruct the model to only surface unresolved or new issues.
D. Implement a hash-based deduplication system that persists finding fingerprints between consecutive runs and automatically filters identical results.

question7.question: A team addresses duplicate review comments by adding a post-processing step that compares new findings to previous ones by file path and description, suppressing matches. A month later, developers report that real regressions—fixed code that broke again—are being silently suppressed. What is the flaw in this approach?
answers: A. The comparison algorithm is too strict; it should match on file path only, not description.
B. The approach is fundamentally sound; the team simply needs to tune the matching threshold.
C. Post-processing runs after review, so it doesn't reduce the number of tokens sent to the model.
D. Post-processing deduplication can't distinguish between a truly resolved issue and a regression that looks identical.

question7.question: In a multi-turn automated review workflow where the same codebase is analyzed repeatedly as changes are applied, what is the most effective mechanism to prevent redundant findings?
answers: A. Implement a content-hash system that identifies unchanged code blocks and skips them.
B. Cache all previous findings and refuse to re-analyze files not changed since the last review.
C. Feed prior findings as context and instruct the model to distinguish new issues from already-identified ones.
D. Use a separate summarization pass to collapse duplicate findings after each review run.

question8.question: Your automated code review averages 15 findings per pull request, with developers reporting a 40% false positive rate. The bottleneck is investigation time: developers must click into each finding to read Claude's reasoning before deciding whether to address or dismiss it. Your CLAUDE.md already contains comprehensive rules for acceptable patterns, and stakeholders have rejected any approach that filters findings before developer review. What change would best address the investigation time bottleneck?
answers: A. Categorize findings as 'blocking issues' versus 'suggestions' with tiered review requirements.
B. Require Claude to include its reasoning and confidence assessment inline with each finding.
C. Configure Claude to only surface findings it assesses as high confidence, filtering out uncertain flags before developers see them.
D. Add a post-processor that analyzes finding patterns and automatically suppresses those matching historical false positive signatures.

question8.question: A dependency risk checker flags 20 packages per report. Developers say evaluation takes too long because each flag requires manual research to determine if it's a real risk. Stakeholders insist all flagged packages must remain visible. What change best speeds up triage?
answers: A. Reduce the volume of flagged packages by raising the internal confidence threshold, accepting fewer but higher-confidence flags per report.
B. Group flagged packages by their vulnerability type category to reduce cognitive load developers experience when switching between different risk types.
C. Add a single-click dismissal button per finding that records developer feedback and feeds it into the model's ongoing calibration and confidence scoring.
D. Include model reasoning and confidence level alongside each flagged package so developers can quickly assess credibility without manual research.

question8.question: A developer proposes fixing the investigation time problem by setting a high confidence threshold so Claude only shows findings it's 'very sure' about. A stakeholder rejects this because it might suppress real bugs. The developer then proposes showing all findings but adding color-coding by severity. Why does this fail to address the root bottleneck?
answers: A. Color-coding by severity is not natively supported by the code review platform's API and requires building a custom rendering extension.
B. Color-coding severity levels adds an additional visual dimension developers must interpret, increasing overall cognitive load and slowing reviews further.
C. Severity tells developers what matters most but doesn't explain whether each finding is valid, which is the actual investigation cost.
D. Color-coding would fully resolve the investigation time problem; the stakeholder objection about potential real bug suppression is technically unfounded.

question8.question: When developer triage of automated findings takes too long and you cannot reduce the number of findings shown, what information addition most directly reduces per-finding evaluation time?
answers: A. Linking each finding to its relevant coding standard documentation so developers can immediately verify whether the guideline applies to their case.
B. Including the model's reasoning and confidence level with each finding so developers can quickly judge its validity.
C. Grouping findings by source file so developers can process all findings for a given file in a single focused review session.
D. Appending an estimated fix-time to each finding so developers can prioritize their review queue by total remediation effort.

question9.question: Your pipeline script runs `claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues"` but the job hangs indefinitely. Logs indicate Claude Code is waiting for interactive input. What's the correct approach to run Claude Code in an automated pipeline?
answers: A. Add the `-p` flag: `claude -p "Analyze this pull request for security issues"`
B. Set the environment variable `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` before running the command.
C. Redirect stdin from `/dev/null`: `claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues" < /dev/null`
D. Add the `--batch` flag: `claude --batch "Analyze this pull request for security issues"`

question9.question: A GitHub Actions workflow step runs `claude "Generate a changelog from these commits"` and the step never exits. The runner eventually times out. What is the correct command for a non-interactive CI environment?
answers: A. `claude --ci "Generate a changelog from these commits"`
B. `claude --non-interactive "Generate a changelog from these commits"`
C. `CLAUDE_AUTO_CONFIRM=true claude "Generate a changelog from these commits"`
D. `claude -p "Generate a changelog from these commits"`

question9.question: A developer redirects stdin from `/dev/null` to prevent Claude Code from waiting for interactive input in CI: `claude "Review this code" < /dev/null`. The job still hangs. Why didn't this work?
answers: A. Stdin `/dev/null` redirection works in bash but is silently ignored in the POSIX sh shell that most CI runners use, which handles null device redirection differently.
B. The correct approach is to use `/dev/zero` as the stdin source, which provides an infinite stream of null bytes that properly suppresses all interactive prompts.
C. The stdin redirection is functioning correctly and the hang must be caused by a separate configuration issue unrelated to Claude Code's input handling.
D. Claude Code's interactive mode is triggered by TTY detection, not stdin availability; the `-p` flag is required to enable print/headless mode.

question9.question: When integrating the Claude Code CLI into an automated, non-interactive pipeline, which flag is required to prevent the tool from blocking on interactive prompts?
answers: A. `--headless`
B. `--auto-confirm`
C. `-p` (print mode)
D. `--batch`

question10.question: Your CI pipeline runs the Claude Code CLI (with --print mode) using CLAUDE.md to provide project context for code reviews, and developers generally find the reviews insightful. However, they report that integrating findings into your workflow is difficult—Claude produces narrative paragraphs that must be manually copied into PR comments. Your team wants to automatically post each finding as a separate inline PR comment at the relevant code location, which requires structured data with file path, line number, severity, and suggested fix. What's the most effective approach?
answers: A. Use CLI flags `--output-format json` and `--json-schema` to enforce structured findings, then parse output to post inline comments via the GitHub API.
B. Include explicit per-finding formatting instructions in your review prompt requiring each finding to follow a structured template with file path, line number, severity, and suggested fix fields.
C. Keep the narrative review format but add a secondary processing call that converts the prose output into structured JSON with all required fields before posting to GitHub.
D. Add a dedicated 'Review Output Format' section to CLAUDE.md with fully annotated examples of correctly structured findings so Claude infers the expected schema from project context.

question10.question: A Claude Code CLI workflow generates deployment risk summaries as prose. Your SRE team wants to pipe these into a dashboard that requires structured JSON with fields: `service`, `risk_level`, `reason`, `recommended_action`. What is the correct approach?
answers: A. Add 'respond only in JSON with fields: service, risk_level, reason, recommended_action' to the prompt and parse the output with a lenient JSON parser that strips surrounding prose.
B. Route the prose output through a secondary Claude call that extracts the required fields and returns them in the JSON format the SRE dashboard expects.
C. Add a representative example JSON response to CLAUDE.md so Claude infers the expected output format from project-level context rather than prompt instructions.
D. Pass a JSON schema via `--json-schema` and set `--output-format json` to enforce structured output at the CLI level.

question10.question: A developer adds detailed prompt instructions: 'Respond only in JSON. Each finding must include file, line, severity, and fix keys.' Output is JSON-shaped sometimes but still occasionally includes prose introductions or markdown fences. What is the more reliable solution?
answers: A. Add stricter prohibitive instructions to the prompt — 'Do not include any prose, markdown, or text outside the JSON structure' — to prevent extraneous formatting.
B. Migrate the implementation to the direct API endpoint where JSON output mode is enforced at the request level and behaves more reliably than CLI instructions.
C. Build a validation wrapper that parses each response and automatically re-invokes the command whenever the output contains non-JSON content, retrying until clean.
D. Use `--output-format json` and `--json-schema` flags, which enforce structure at the CLI level rather than relying on instruction-following.

question10.question: When you need Claude Code CLI output to conform to a specific machine-readable schema for downstream processing, what is the most reliable enforcement mechanism compared to prompt instructions?
answers: A. Add a fully specified JSON schema directly to the system prompt as a formatting reference so the model can replicate the expected output structure.
B. Use CLI-level schema enforcement flags (`--output-format`, `--json-schema`) that constrain the output format structurally.
C. Build retry logic with output validation that re-invokes the command automatically whenever the model produces non-conforming output.
D. Collect labeled examples of the desired structured output and fine-tune the model specifically for JSON generation in code review contexts.

question11.question: Your automated review generates test case suggestions for each PR. When reviewing a PR that adds course completion tracking, Claude suggests 10 test cases but developer feedback indicates 6 duplicate scenarios already covered in the existing test suite. What change would most effectively reduce duplicate suggestions?
answers: A. Add a post-processing filter that suppresses suggestions whose descriptions contain keywords already present in the names of existing test functions.
B. Add instructions directing Claude to generate only edge-case failure scenarios, on the assumption that all standard happy-path coverage already exists in the test suite.
C. Reduce requested suggestions from 10 to 5, assuming Claude will naturally surface only the most valuable and non-redundant test cases when given fewer slots.
D. Include the existing test file in the context so Claude can identify what scenarios are already covered.

question11.question: An AI-powered feature specification tool generates requirements for a new module but 40% of the suggestions duplicate requirements already documented in the existing spec. The prompt says 'generate comprehensive requirements.' What is the most direct fix?
answers: A. Add the instruction 'avoid duplicating requirements already listed' to the prompt and have Claude review its output for overlap before finalizing the suggestions.
B. Run a post-generation deduplication pass that compares each newly generated requirement against the existing specification and removes any semantic matches.
C. Include the existing specification document in the prompt context so the model can see what already exists.
D. Ask the model to generate only 'novel' requirements not typically found in standard implementations, to reduce overlap with the existing documented specification.

question11.question: To fix duplicate test suggestions, a developer adds the instruction 'only suggest test cases that are not already covered in the existing test suite.' Duplicates persist. Why didn't this instruction work?
answers: A. The model systematically disregards negative exclusion constraints during generation, making all instruction-based approaches to preventing duplication ineffective.
B. Without the actual test file in context, the model has no way to know what tests already exist—the instruction is unfulfillable.
C. The instruction fundamentally conflicts with the model's training objective to produce comprehensive outputs, so it is systematically overridden during generation.
D. The instruction would have been more effective if phrased positively as 'only generate test cases not present in the existing test suite.'

question11.question: A code generation assistant consistently produces suggestions that duplicate existing implementations because the existing code is not included in the prompt. What is the most direct fix?
answers: A. Add explicit instructions directing Claude to avoid common standard-library implementations and focus only on project-specific logic not present in typical codebases.
B. Ask the model to explain and justify each suggestion individually, allowing you to review and filter out recommendations that duplicate existing code.
C. Reduce the total number of suggestions requested per prompt, on the assumption that a smaller target output reduces overlap probability.
D. Include the existing codebase (or the relevant portion of it) as context before generating suggestions.

question12.question: Your CI pipeline includes two Claude-powered code review modes: a pre-merge-commit hook that blocks PR merging until complete, and 'deep analysis' that runs overnight, polls for batch completion, then posts detailed suggestions to the PR. You want to reduce API costs using the Message Batches API, which offers 50% cost savings but requires polling and may take up to 24 hours to complete. Which mode should use batch processing?
answers: A. Deep analysis only
B. Neither mode
C. Both modes
D. Pre-merge-commit hook only

question12.question: A platform runs two Claude jobs: (1) an instant code explanation shown in the IDE as developers type, (2) a weekly architecture quality report sent to tech leads on Mondays. The Batch API offers 50% cost reduction with up to 24-hour processing time. Which job should use batch processing?
answers: A. Both jobs — cost savings apply equally to both.
B. Neither — the 24-hour delay is unacceptable for both.
C. Weekly architecture report only.
D. IDE code explanation only.

question12.question: A developer applies batch processing to both their pre-merge code quality gate and their monthly compliance report to maximize the 50% cost savings. The next morning, 30 pull requests are stuck open. What was the mistake?
answers: A. The developer forgot to configure polling and the pipeline never received the batch results.
B. The Batch API has a queue limit that was exceeded by 30 simultaneous requests.
C. The code quality gate needs streaming, not batch; only reporting tasks support batch processing.
D. Batch processing was applied to a blocking, latency-sensitive task that required synchronous real-time results.

question12.question: Given two automated tasks—one that blocks a human action until complete, and one that produces a report consumed the next business day—which should use asynchronous batch processing?
answers: A. Both — async processing is always preferable for cost efficiency.
B. The blocking task — it benefits more from the cost savings.
C. The next-day report task only, since it has inherent latency tolerance.
D. Neither — asynchronous processing introduces ordering issues in both cases.

question13.question: Your team uses Claude Code to generate code suggestions, but you notice a pattern: subtle issues—performance optimizations that break edge cases, cleanups that change behavior unexpectedly—only surface when a different team member reviews the PR. Claude's reasoning during generation shows it considered these cases but concluded its approach was correct. Which approach directly addresses the root cause of this self-review limitation?
answers: A. Enable extended thinking mode for the generation pass, allowing more thorough deliberation before producing suggestions.
B. Add explicit self-review instructions to the generation prompt, asking Claude to critique its own suggestions before finalizing output.
C. Include comprehensive test files and documentation in the prompt context so Claude better understands expected behavior during generation.
D. Have a second, independent Claude Code instance review the changes without seeing the generator's reasoning.

question13.question: An LLM generates a data migration script and then reviews its own output for errors. The review passes it as correct. A human engineer later finds a data type mismatch that the generator 'considered but ruled out' in its chain of thought. What architectural change would catch such issues?
answers: A. Apply chain-of-thought prompting to require the generator to explicitly document its design decisions and reasoning before producing the final output.
B. Add a pre-finalization step where the generator enumerates all potential issues with its own output and addresses each one before submitting.
C. Pass the script to a second LLM instance that has no access to the first instance's reasoning trace.
D. Increase the generation temperature to introduce output variance, enabling the team to compare multiple diverse candidate scripts.

question13.question: A team adds the instruction 'After generating code, critically review it for edge cases you may have missed.' Issues that were considered and dismissed during generation still pass the self-review. Why?
answers: A. The self-review step executes in the same context as generation, inheriting the same reasoning biases and prior commitments.
B. The self-review instruction is grammatically ambiguous and must be restructured as two clearly separated sentences to take effect.
C. The model lacks access to test execution results at review time, which are required to identify which edge cases actually fail in the generated code.
D. Self-critique only produces reliable results when chain-of-thought reasoning is explicitly enabled; the team should prepend 'think step by step' to the instruction.

question13.question: Why is a second independent LLM instance more effective than self-review for catching subtle errors in generated content?
answers: A. Running two instances effectively doubles the total context window available, enabling more thorough analysis than a single instance can produce alone.
B. The second instance accesses a freshly populated cache from the start, which reduces processing time and produces statistically faster review results.
C. Two instances initialized with different random seeds produce more diverse outputs, increasing the probability that at least one identifies the critical issue.
D. An independent instance hasn't committed to the generator's reasoning, so it can identify flaws the generator rationalized away.

question14.question: Your team wants to reduce API costs for automated analysis. Currently, real-time Claude calls power two workflows: (1) a blocking pre-merge check that must complete before developers can merge, and (2) a technical debt report generated overnight for review the next morning. Your manager proposes switching both to the Message Batches API for its 50% cost savings. How should you evaluate this proposal?
answers: A. Switch both workflows to batch processing with status polling to check for completion.
B. Use batch processing for the technical debt reports only; keep real-time calls for pre-merge checks.
C. Switch both to batch processing with a timeout fallback to real-time if batches take too long.
D. Keep real-time calls for both workflows to avoid batch result ordering issues.

question14.question: A company runs two AI analysis jobs: a fraud detection check that approves or declines transactions in real time, and a monthly spending pattern analysis emailed to finance. To cut LLM costs by 50%, the CTO proposes switching both to batch processing. What is the correct response?
answers: A. Switch both — the cost savings justify accepting longer processing times for both workflows.
B. Switch only fraud detection — it generates more volume and therefore higher absolute cost savings.
C. Keep both on real-time — batch processing lacks sufficient reliability for financial workflows.
D. Switch only the monthly spending analysis; real-time fraud detection requires synchronous API calls.

question14.question: A developer argues: 'We should keep both workflows real-time because the 50% batch savings don't justify the added complexity of polling and async handling.' What is the flaw in this reasoning?
answers: A. The developer is entirely correct — the operational complexity of implementing reliable polling and async handling always outweighs any cost savings the batch discount provides.
B. The developer ignores that one workflow already has inherent overnight latency tolerance, making added polling complexity minimal and cost savings significant for that task.
C. Batch processing eliminates the need for polling entirely because completed results are automatically pushed via webhook callbacks rather than requiring status checks.
D. The developer's cost-benefit argument is technically sound; the decision to migrate depends entirely on each organization's specific infrastructure and tolerance for complexity.

question14.question: When evaluating a proposal to migrate LLM API calls to batch processing for cost savings, what single factor determines whether the migration is appropriate for a given workflow?
answers: A. The total request volume of the workflow, since high-frequency tasks generate the greatest absolute token savings from the batch processing discount.
B. The average prompt length submitted, since longer prompts save more tokens per call and yield higher absolute cost reductions at scale.
C. Whether the workflow has a hard real-time requirement that would be violated by batch latency.
D. The target model version, since only specific model releases include the optimizations required to make batch processing efficient and reliable.

question15.question: Analysis of your automated code review shows significant variation in false positive rates across finding categories. Security and correctness findings have an 8% false positive rate, performance findings have 18%, style and naming findings have 52%, and documentation findings have 48%. Developer surveys indicate growing distrust—many have started dismissing findings without review because 'half are wrong.' The high false positive categories are undermining confidence in the accurate categories. What approach best restores developer trust while improving the system?
answers: A. Apply a uniform strictness reduction across all categories to bring the overall false positive rate to an acceptable level.
B. Temporarily disable high false positive categories (style, naming, documentation) and run only high-precision categories while improving prompts.
C. Keep all categories but display a confidence score with each finding, letting developers decide which to investigate.
D. Keep all categories enabled while adding few-shot examples to improve each category's accuracy over the coming weeks.

question15.question: An automated PR labeling system has four label types: 'breaking change' (5% FP), 'security risk' (10% FP), 'cosmetic only' (60% FP), 'performance impact' (55% FP). Developers ignore all labels because the inaccurate ones undermine credibility. What is the best recovery strategy?
answers: A. Lower the internal confidence threshold uniformly across all four label types to reduce the overall false positive rate and produce fewer but more reliable predictions.
B. Disable 'cosmetic only' and 'performance impact' labels until accuracy improves; continue using 'breaking change' and 'security risk.'
C. Enrich the prompt with additional context and examples for each label type to improve the model's discriminative ability between closely related categories.
D. Display all labels but mark predictions from the two underperforming types with a visible '(low confidence)' indicator for developer awareness.

question15.question: To address low developer trust from high false positive rates in style and documentation categories, a team displays a confidence score with every finding so developers can decide what to investigate. Six weeks later, developer engagement with all categories has dropped further. Why did the confidence score approach fail?
answers: A. The model's confidence scores are systematically miscalibrated and do not correlate reliably with whether individual findings in those categories are actually accurate.
B. The confidence score display was too complex for developers to interpret quickly during triage, slowing down individual finding evaluations rather than accelerating them.
C. The approach would have been effective if confidence scores had been shown selectively, only for findings from the two high false-positive categories.
D. Displaying confidence scores alongside inaccurate categories still requires developers to process findings from those categories, maintaining triage burden and distrust.

question15.question: When one component of an automated system has high error rates that are causing users to distrust the entire system, what is the most effective immediate strategy to protect confidence in the system's accurate components?
answers: A. Communicate clearly about known limitations and ask users to be patient while improvements are made.
B. Reduce output from all components equally so users see fewer total results.
C. Isolate the inaccurate component from user-facing output while maintaining the high-precision components.
D. Display error rates alongside outputs so users can calibrate their trust appropriately.
